title: Toyota 4Runner 1st Gen
verdict: A Hilux pickup with a removable fibreglass hat, a four-cylinder that refuses to die and — for 1984–85 only — a solid front axle. Slow, rusty, uncomfortable and utterly charming, which is exactly why the prices went up.

paragraphs: The first 4Runner was less designed than improvised: take Toyota's redesigned 1984 Hilux 4x4 pickup, give the bed a fibreglass lid and a back seat (sometimes), and ship it to America. It went on sale in the US in May 1984 as a 1984½ model — two doors, a four-cylinder, a five-speed and, for its first two seasons, a solid front axle on leaf springs. Four decades on it is the 4Runner people call 'pure', and the one Hagerty says can't be ignored now that clean examples keep getting more expensive.

story.heading: A PICKUP WITH A HAT
paragraphs: Toyota had already seen the idea work. Between 1981 and 1983 Winnebago and Toyota turned short-bed Hilux 4x4s into the Trekker — a fibreglass-lined bed, an extra seat and a fibreglass top — and Curbside Classic counts only around 1,500 of them. The factory version arrived as the Hilux Surf in Japan in October 1983 and as the 4Runner in North America a few months later, just as the FJ40 [[land-cruiser/fj40|Land Cruiser]] left the US market and the small-SUV class filled up with the S-10 Blazer, Bronco II and Jeep Cherokee.

Hagerty describes the details that make owners grin: a rear roof held on by 14 bolts, a standard rear roll bar, and a power rear window that drops into the tailgate. SR5s added an altimeter and inclinometer on the dash, a rear seat, strobe-stripe graphics and chrome wheels; the base DX often came without a rear seat at all, and Toyota never fitted rear shoulder belts.

story.heading: ENGINES, AND THE AXLE ARGUMENT
paragraphs: The 1984½ trucks used the carburetted 2.4-litre 22R making 96 hp, paired only with a five-speed. Fuel injection arrived for 1985 as the 22R-E — Wikipedia lists 116 hp — and 1986 brought the 135 hp 22R-TE turbo, mostly sold with the automatic in SR5s and far rarer than the plain 22R-E. For 1988 the 3.0-litre 3VZ-E V6 joined the range, rated at 145–150 hp depending on the source. Hagerty's verdict on the whole run: 0–60 times improved 'from months to weeks to about 12 seconds'.

The bigger change came underneath. For 1986 the solid front axle was replaced by independent front suspension with a three-inch-wider track, which made the truck calmer on the road and, by most accounts, a little less heroic off it. That split defines the generation today: 1984–85 trucks are the solid-axle purist's choice, while 1986–89 trucks ride better and share their front end with the [[4runner/2nd-gen|second generation]]. Both keep a leaf-sprung rear axle that Wikipedia notes was never upgraded for the extra weight of the seats and top — so sagging is normal.

story.heading: WHY IT MATTERS NOW
paragraphs: In its own time the N60 was a slow starter: US sales were 6,498 in 1984 and dipped below 4,000 in 1987, before jumping to 20,880 in 1988 and 36,927 in calendar 1989 (a figure that includes the first 2nd gens). Today the story has flipped. Hagerty reported average values of $8,400 in #3 condition, $13,700 in #2 and $21,100 in #1, with Bring a Trailer sales of a 100,000-mile 1984 SR5 at $19,250, and found that millennials and Gen-Xers made up a far larger share of 4Runner insurance quotes than of the market overall.

The Autopian's David Tracy goes further, naming the 1985 — fuel-injected, solid-axled, convertible-topped and under 3,500 lb — his perfect 4Runner. The catch is survival. Open tops let water in, floors and quarter panels are not reproduced, and Hagerty notes that original seats and upholstery are close to unobtainable. Mechanically, though, the 22R-family engines are among the easiest Toyota ever built, and LC Engineering still runs a whole 1984–1989 4Runner catalogue.

story.heading: THE AFTERMATH
paragraphs: For 1990 Toyota replaced it with a four-door, fixed-roof [[4runner/2nd-gen|second generation]] that kept the independent front end and swapped the rear leafs for coils. The removable top never returned, and by the [[4runner/3rd-gen|third generation]] the pickup-with-a-lid idea had vanished entirely. The first gen became something else: the cheap, simple base for solid-axle swaps, V8 conversions and camper builds — Expedition Portal's classifieds once listed a 1985 SR5 on Old Man Emu springs with a FlipPac pop-up roof for $8,000. Nobody is building them that way from new any more, which is rather the point.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · BEFORE THE 4RUNNER
callout.title: The Trekker: Winnebago's 4Runner prototype you could buy
paragraphs: Before Toyota built its own 4Runner, Winnebago did a version for it. Curbside Classic describes how short-bed Toyota 4x4 pickups were sent to Winnebago, which lined the bed with fibreglass, added a seat and fitted a fibreglass top; 'only some 1500 Trekkers were made and sold, between 1981 and 1983'.

Its true origins are hazy, and Curbside Classic found no evidence that the Trekker's top was meant to come off. But the concept — Hilux 4x4 plus enclosed back with seats — is exactly what Toyota put into production for 1984. LC Engineering still lists the 1981–1983 Trekker as its own model in its parts catalogue.

engineering_intro: Mechanically the N60 is a Toyota Hilux 4x4 pickup, nearly part-for-part. That means a ladder frame, a leaf-sprung live rear axle, a part-time transfer case and an engine bay designed for the simple 22R family. The interesting choices are the 1984–85 solid front axle with manual locking hubs, the switch to torsion-bar independent front suspension for 1986, and a removable fibreglass rear roof.

engineering.note: Nearly mechanically identical to the 1984-on Hilux pickup.
Leaf-sprung solid axle with manual hubs 1984–85; torsion-bar IFS with a 3 in wider track from 1986.
Hotchkiss drive; springs weren't uprated for the seats and top, so they sag.
Carburetted 22R in 1984; EFI from 1985; turbo 22R-TE from 1986; 3VZ-E V6 from 1988.
Manual locking hubs; automatic hubs added to SR5s for 1988.
Fibreglass rear roof held by 14 bolts, standard roll bar, power tailgate glass.

generations_table.note: Five-speed manual only. DX or SR5.
Fuel injection arrives; the last solid-axle year.
IFS with 3 in wider track; two-segment grille from 1986.
Mostly automatic SR5s; much rarer than the 22R-E.
Optional V6; auto hubs on SR5s. Sales take off.

buying_checks.head: Rust, everywhere
buying_checks.body: Forum owners point to the frame ahead of the rear spring perches, the rear quarters and wheel wells, the left rear near the exhaust exit, and, on sunroof-equipped trucks, A-pillars that owners say rotted from blocked drains. Hagerty warns that floors and quarter panels aren't reproduced, so a rusty body is a fabrication job, not a parts order.

buying_checks.head: Know which axle you're buying
buying_checks.body: 1984–85 trucks have the solid front axle; 1986–89 have IFS. Solid-axle trucks carry a price premium and some sellers stretch the truth, so look underneath: leaf springs and manual hubs up front mean solid axle; torsion bars and CV axles mean IFS.

buying_checks.head: 22R-E timing chain guides
buying_checks.body: The plastic timing-chain guides are a known breakage item — LC Engineering makes metal-backed replacements specifically for it. A cold-start rattle from the front of the engine, or no record of the job, means budget for chain, guides and tensioner.

buying_checks.head: V6 head gaskets
buying_checks.body: The 1988–89 3VZ-E shares the V6's head-gasket reputation. Toyota's October 1996 policy adjustment (1988–94 V6 trucks) is long expired and the later V06 campaign only covered 1/90–10/94 builds, so check for coolant loss, overheating history and white exhaust, and ask for paperwork on any head work.

buying_checks.head: Sagging rear and tired suspension
buying_checks.body: Rear leafs sag on nearly all of them. Feathered front tyres can mean worn front-end parts or a bad alignment; on IFS trucks check idler arm and tie-rod play.

buying_checks.head: Top, glass and seals
buying_checks.body: Removable tops and ageing seals leak; a tarp over the roof in the ad is a clue. Check the power tailgate window works — IH8MUD members flag it as a weak point on both early generations.

buying_checks.head: Interior parts
buying_checks.body: Carpets can be found, but Hagerty says reproduction seats and upholstery generally can't, and owners say good seats are especially scarce. An intact original interior is worth paying for.

buying_checks.head: Rear seats and belts
buying_checks.body: Many 1984–86 base trucks came without a rear seat, and Toyota never fitted rear shoulder belts. If you plan to carry kids, factor that in.

repairs.title: 22R-E timing chain, guides and tensioner
repairs.time: Most of a weekend for a first-timer
repairs.cost: Metal-backed guides ≈ $64 (LC Engineering), plus chain, tensioner and gaskets
repairs.symptoms: Rattle or slap from the timing cover at start-up, broken guide pieces in the oil pan, or simply no record that it's ever been done.
repairs.fix: Drain coolant, remove the fan, radiator and accessories, then the timing cover. Fit the new guides positioned toward the outside of the block without tightening, install the crank gear, then the cam gear and chain with the bright link on top. Tighten the straight guide to 9 ft-lb, install the tensioner (also 9 ft-lb), position the curved guide toward the outside so the tensioner is mostly retracted, torque everything and refit the cam gear (per LC Engineering's instructions). Reassemble with a new cover gasket set.
repairs.tools: Metric sockets · torque wrench · gasket scraper · LCE metal-backed guides (single row, 1985–95) · timing chain · tensioner · timing cover gasket set

repairs.title: 3VZ-E head gaskets (1988–89 V6)
repairs.time: Several days; heads usually go to a machine shop
repairs.cost: MLS head gasket set ≈ $116 (LC Engineering), plus machining and a timing belt kit
repairs.symptoms: Coolant loss with no visible leak, white exhaust after warm-up, overheating, misfires — 4Runners.com members say cylinder 6 is the usual victim.
repairs.fix: This is an engine-out-of-the-car level job in all but name: drain fluids, strip the intake and exhaust crossover, remove the timing belt and cams, pull both heads and have them checked flat. Fit MLS gaskets (they need a very smooth deck finish), new head bolts or studs, and do the timing belt, water pump and thermostat while it's apart. Many owners add an exhaust crossover delete to reduce heat at the back of the engine.
repairs.tools: Full metric socket set · torque wrench · cam/crank pulley tools · LCE MLS head gasket set · 3VZ OE head bolt set (88–95) · 3VZ timing belt kit (1988–92)

parts.name: Water pump — 3VZ (LCE lists 1989–92; confirm fit on 1988 trucks)

repairs.title: Rear leaf spring replacement
repairs.symptoms: Rear sitting low or level with the front, bottoming out over bumps, cracked or flattened leaves.
repairs.fix: Support the frame on stands and take the weight off the axle with a jack. Remove the shocks' lower mounts, the U-bolts and spring plate, then the shackle and front hanger bolts. Swap in new springs (LC Engineering sells 1984–89 4Runner sets at +2, +3 and +4 in) with new bushings, refit the U-bolts and torque everything with the truck back on its wheels so the bushings aren't preloaded.
repairs.tools: Floor jack · stands · breaker bar · penetrating oil · new U-bolts · LCE 1984–89 4Runner rear leaf spring set

repairs.title: IFS idler arm and steering slop (1986–89)
repairs.cost: Parts plus labor; a Total Chaos 'Caddy' idler arm costs more than a stock one
repairs.symptoms: Wander on the highway, play at the wheel, a clunk over bumps, especially on bigger tyres.
repairs.fix: With the front supported, check for play at the idler arm, tie-rod ends and pitman arm. To replace the idler arm, separate the centre link from it with a puller, unbolt it from the frame and fit the new one, then re-torque and get an alignment. IH8MUD members recommend a stronger idler arm or brace on any IFS truck that sees off-road use.
repairs.tools: Pitman/tie-rod puller · torque wrench · Total Chaos Caddy idler arm 95130 (1986–95 4Runner) or OEM-type arm

repairs.title: Solid-axle front end refresh (1984–85)
repairs.symptoms: Grease or gear oil weeping from the knuckles, wheel bearing play, clicking from worn birfields on tight turns in 4WD.
repairs.fix: Pull the hubs, spindles and birfield axles, clean and inspect the joints, then replace wheel bearings and seals and rebuild the knuckles (trunnion bearings and wiper seals). Repack with fresh grease and set bearing preload on reassembly. Trail-Gear's Classic front lift kit for 1979–85 solid-axle trucks bundles a knuckle rebuild kit and wheel bearing kits for exactly this reason.
repairs.tools: Hub socket · slide hammer · snap-ring pliers · knuckle rebuild kit · wheel bearing kits · Longfield or RCV axle upgrades if you're running bigger tyres

parts.name: Solid axle knuckle service kit with wheel bearings
Toyota knuckle rebuild kit (Japanese trunnion bearings)

repairs.title: Sunroof drain and leak control
repairs.cost: Next to nothing — until it rots an A-pillar
repairs.symptoms: On sunroof-equipped trucks: wet headliner or carpets, rust bubbling at the base of the A-pillars, a musty cab.
repairs.fix: Owners report blocked sunroof drains rusting out A-pillars on trucks fitted with a sunroof. Clear the drain tubes with trimmer line or low-pressure air, check the outlets aren't crushed, and replace hardened top and window seals. Treat any surface rust in the pillars before it goes through.
repairs.tools: Trimmer line · low-pressure air · rust converter · new seals

repairs.title: Swap failing auto hubs for manual hubs
repairs.time: An afternoon, including a bearing repack
repairs.cost: Aisin manual hubs ≈ $249 a set (1986–95 IFS) or ≈ $415 a pair (1979–85 solid axle), plus a ≈ $28 conversion kit (LC Engineering)
repairs.symptoms: Front hubs that won't lock, slip under load or let go in reverse. 4Runners.com notes the auto hubs fitted to some 1984–89 4Runners are less reliable than manual hubs and will sometimes unlock in reverse.
repairs.fix: Confirm you have auto hubs (no dial to turn on the hub cap). Remove the auto hub assemblies and the auto-hub hardware on the spindle. Fit LC Engineering's conversion kit: the locking nuts and plates that hold the hub and rotor on the spindle once the auto-hub parts are gone. Repack the wheel bearings and set the preload to the factory manual while it's apart, then fit the manual hubs on new gaskets. Solid-axle (1984–85) and IFS (1986–89) hubs have different spline counts, so order the right ones.
repairs.tools: Sockets · spindle-nut socket · snap-ring pliers · torque wrench · wheel-bearing grease and new seals

parts.name: Aisin manual locking hubs, 1979–85 solid axle (pair)

repairs.title: Power tailgate window that sticks or drops
repairs.cost: Parts plus labor; one Toyota-4Runner.org member recommends a used motor
repairs.symptoms: The roll-down rear glass works only some of the time, stalls part-way or suddenly drops into the tailgate. IH8MUD members flag the electric rear window as a weak point on both early generations; Toyota-4Runner.org owners trace it to tired motors, regulator gears and drag in the channels.
repairs.fix: Pull the tailgate's inner access panels. Run the glass up and down and check it stays in its tracks, then push and twist the regulator to see whether its gears stay meshed. If the regulator is sound, test the motor directly on a battery, then check the relay. Clean the channels and put silicone spray on the glass edges and rubber seals; one owner says a dealer clean-and-lube cured his. Toyota-4Runner.org members describe the motors as easily overwhelmed by drag, and one says 1st and 2nd gen motors are the same apart from the connector plug. If the glass has dropped and broken before, check the regulator was actually fixed, not just the glass.
repairs.tools: Trim-panel tools · screwdrivers · 12 V jumper leads · multimeter · silicone spray

parts.name: Tailgate window motor and regulator (RockAuto catalogue)

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: Owners' consensus is 31x10.50R15 — Toyota-4Runner.org members say 31s fit with no lift and you can get away without regearing. 33x12.50s on a stock truck rub the front valance, wheel-well corners and rear pinch weld; IH8MUD owners estimate about 1.5 in of lift (plus some trimming) for 33s, and say the 22R-E will want lower gears.

faq.q: Which years have the solid front axle?
faq.a: 1984 and 1985. Toyota switched to independent front suspension with a three-inch-wider track for 1986, so 1986–89 trucks are IFS. Solid-axle trucks are the off-roader's favourite; IFS trucks ride better on the road.

Most enthusiasts prefer the 22R-E four-cylinder — Hagerty says so, and Expedition Portal members advise skipping the V6. The 3.0 V6 (1988–89) has more power but carries the 3VZ-E's head-gasket reputation and is harder to work on; the 22R-E is slow but famously simple.

faq.q: Can I take the roof off?
faq.a: Yes. The rear fibreglass top is held on by 14 bolts, and a rear roll bar was standard. Owners note the open-top experience mostly benefits rear passengers — and that ageing tops are a common leak point.
Not in the US. Diesel engines were offered in Hilux pickups, but Wikipedia records that no diesel 4Runners were imported to the US.

The 22R-TE turbo four arrived for 1986 with 135 hp, mostly paired with the four-speed automatic in SR5s. It's much rarer than the 22R-E, and LC Engineering still sells dedicated 22R-TE short blocks and turbo parts.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: Not much. Wikipedia records an EPA city rating of 17 mpg for the 22R-TE turbo truck and 14.5 mpg in period testing; Trail4Runner quotes 19 city / 23 highway for a stock four-cylinder, which looks optimistic. Expect less with bigger tyres, a lift or a tired engine.

faq.q: Is a 1988–89 V6 covered by Toyota's head gasket campaign?
faq.a: Not any more. An October 1996 Special Policy Adjustment extended head-gasket coverage for 1988–1994 V6 trucks; the later V06 campaign covered 1/90–10/94 production and expired on 24 September 2018. Today a blown 3VZ-E head gasket is on you.

Hagerty's write-up on rising 1984–89 values gave averages of $8,400 (#3 Good), $13,700 (#2 Excellent) and $21,100 (#1 Concours), and cited Bring a Trailer sales of $19,250 for a 100,000-mile 1984 SR5 and $17,500 for a 168,000-mile 1986 SR5. Expedition Portal members reckoned a maintained 22R-E truck under about 170,000 miles could still be found for under $5,000.

faq.q: Should I solid-axle swap an IFS truck?
faq.a: IH8MUD members are split. Some say the 1986–95 Toyota IFS is 'pretty stout' unless you rock-crawl hard; others who broke IFS shafts say to 'spend the money on a SAS and never look back'. Kits for 1979–85-style solid axles, long-travel IFS and stronger axles are all still sold.

Mechanical parts, yes — the 22R family is shared with Toyota pickups and LC Engineering runs a dedicated 1984–1989 4Runner catalogue. Body panels, floors and interior trim are the hard part; Hagerty notes reproduction seats and floors generally don't exist.

faq.q: Which years are the best to buy?
faq.a: For a trail truck, a 1985: it's the last year of the solid front axle that Hagerty says purists still seek out, and it gets the fuel-injected 22R-E — an Expedition Portal member rates carbureted trucks less desirable. For a daily driver, several of the same forum's members point to a 1986–89 IFS truck with the 22R-E and a manual. Skip the 1988–89 V6: Hagerty's expert says most enthusiasts avoid it in favour of the four. Rust decides more than the model year does.

baseline_service.intro: Assume nothing on a 35-plus-year-old truck: baseline every fluid, filter and wear item the day you buy it, then keep records. Factory capacities and fluid grades for the N60 aren't reliably published online. Figures marked AMSOIL come from AMSOIL's application guide for the 1987 22R-E, and plug data from Denso's catalogue; check those and anything still marked below against the owner's or factory service manual, and know which hubs and axle you have before ordering parts.

items.spec: 22R-E: 10W-30, 10W-40 or 10W-50 above −23 °C (15W-40 to 20W-50 above −12 °C) · ≈4.5 US qt with filter (AMSOIL, 1987 22R-E) · 3VZ-E V6 [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]

items.note: Watch for a 22R-E burning oil at high mileage; leaks often come from the valve cover gasket.
